newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court allows adult cable TV restrictions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court allows adult cable TV restrictions.

text.p: The Supreme Court on Monday upheld part of a 1996 federal law that placed new restrictions on sexually explicit programmes shown on selected cable television channels.

The high court rejected appeals by a Playboy Enterprises Inc. subsidiary and by Spice Entertainment Cos Inc., two companies which provide sexually explicit programming for transmission by cable operators.

Playboy and Spice had sought a preliminary injunction barring implementation and enforcement of one section of the Communications Decency Act, approved by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton in February last year as part of a telecommunications overhaul.

The law requires cable operators that carry channels with mainly sexually explicit programming to take steps to make sure that people who are not subscribers will not receive audio or video signals at a time when children are watching.
The law requires a cable television operator to completely "scramble" or block the video and audio portions of sexually explicit programming, usually shown on pay-per-view channels.

If a cable operator cannot comply with the scrambling requirement, the sexually explicit programming may be shown only when children are unlikely to view it, an eight-hour time period that starts at 10:00 p.m. and ends at 6:00 a.m.

The high court's decision came five days after the justices heard arguments in a historic case involving a separate part of the same law, a section regulating indecent material on the Internet. A ruling in that case is due by July.
Playboy and Spice argued that the law violated First Amendment free-speech guarantees because it subjected protected speech to unconstitutionally vague regulations.
But a three-judge, federal court panel in Delaware last November rejected the arguments, refusing to grant a preliminary injunction blocking the law.

The companies in appealing to the Supreme Court said there were less restrictive measures available to the government and the law unfairly singles out "a handful of targeted cable television channels" for "uniquely unfavourable treatment."
But the Supreme Court sided with the Justice Department, affirming without comment the lower-court judgment and allowing the law to take effect.

In other action, the justices agreed to review a ruling that threw out an $11.3 million award against General Motors Corp. in a product liability case over a 1990 fatal accident involving a Chevrolet Blazer.
The justices agreed to review a U.S. appeals court ruling that overturned a jury verdict favourable to the family of Beverly Garner, a front-seat passenger in the 1985 S-10 Blazer.
She was killed when the vehicle was involved in a head-on collision on a Missouri highway and caught fire. The lawsuit charged the engine fire had been caused by a faulty fuel pump.
But the appeals court overturned the award in June, ruling the jury had not been properly instructed on the issue of punitive damages.
The appeals court said the trial judge wrongly allowed a former GM employee, Ronald Elwell, to testify as a witness for the plaintiffs and it ordered a new trial.

Lawyers for Garner's two sons appealed to the Supreme Court over the issue of whether Elwell should have been barred from testifying. The high court will hear arguments in the case in its term that begins in October, with a decision likely early next year.
